posts.text:
In 1820, roughly one person in eight on Earth could read.

Today it is closer to seven in eight. One map, explained — a thread 🧵🗺️

Data: Our World in Data (CC BY)

1/ The map shows the share of adults who can read and write a simple statement about their everyday life. Dark blue is near-universal. The palest countries — Chad, Mali, Niger, South Sudan, Afghanistan — sit well under half.

2/ First thing to notice: the hatched countries are not missing by accident. The US, Canada, Australia and most of Western Europe stopped reporting a literacy rate because the answer stopped varying. Here, absence means success.

3/ The global adult rate is around 87%. That figure moved further in the last hundred years than in the previous five hundred, and the mechanism is mass schooling — literacy rises when states decide to teach children, not when they get rich.

4/ Latin America is almost uniformly dark now, and was not in 1900. Vietnam and much of Southeast Asia clear 95%. Central Asia is near-universal, a real legacy of Soviet schooling that outlasted the state which built it.
5/ The gap that remains is concentrated in the Sahel and Afghanistan, and it is heavily gendered: roughly two-thirds of adults worldwide who cannot read are women.

6/ Youth literacy runs above adult literacy nearly everywhere, which is the most useful thing this map implies — it tells you where the numbers are heading, not only where they are.

Follow @forummapping for more maps like this.
